buckets.title: Landing page components
buckets.description: Structural building blocks you rearrange to keep a single CTA honest.

terms.title: Hero
terms.shortDescription: The above-the-fold stage that introduces the offer and CTA immediately.
terms.definition: The hero pairs a clear headline, a proof-backed supporting line, and the primary CTA so visitors know what you do and what to do next without scrolling.
terms.whenToUse: Always—the hero is the first impression for any paid or organic visit.
aiPhrases: Draft a hero layout that locks headline, supporting copy, and CTA in a tight Z-pattern.
examples: Headline + subhead on the left, product mock and primary CTA on the right.

terms.title: Subhead
terms.shortDescription: One tight sentence that clarifies value right after the hero headline.
terms.definition: The subhead answers the immediate follow-up question the headline triggers—usually who it is for or what result they get next.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever the headline is bold or outcome-focused and needs context to feel believable.
aiPhrases: Write a subhead that names the audience and promises the outcome in under 18 words.
examples: Designed for growth teams shipping tests weekly

terms.title: Primary CTA
terms.shortDescription: The one action button styled for maximum contrast and clarity.
terms.definition: Your primary CTA uses an action verb, a benefit hint, and surrounding reassurance to make the click feel obvious.
terms.whenToUse: Always present in the hero and repeated within the flow where intent peaks.
aiPhrases: Give me three CTA variants that pair an active verb with the next-step benefit.
examples: Start the 7-day teardown

terms.title: Value props
terms.shortDescription: Three to five punchy proof-backed statements that ladder up to the promise.
terms.definition: Value props are scannable headlines with a short line of support that show how you deliver the main outcome.
terms.whenToUse: Use when visitors need to understand how the product/system works in their context.
aiPhrases: Summarize the top four outcomes as value props with proof metrics or specific details.
examples: Cut build time from weeks to hours with a subline about modular sections

terms.title: Features
terms.shortDescription: Deeper dives that show the mechanics behind each value prop.
terms.definition: Feature blocks combine visuals, captions, and specifics so buyers trust that the promised outcome is doable.
terms.whenToUse: After value props to let detail-oriented readers continue their evaluation.
aiPhrases: Outline three feature cards with titles, supporting copy, and an optional screenshot cue.
examples: Component library, Test dashboard, Collaboration timeline

terms.title: Social proof bar
terms.shortDescription: Logos, usage stats, or quick trust badges that calm hesitation.
terms.definition: A slim strip or cluster that shows recognizable customers, outcomes, or expert quotes without hijacking the main CTA.
terms.whenToUse: Drop near the hero or right before the primary CTA repeats.
aiPhrases: Write a social proof bar headline plus three credibility stats tied to the landing page offer.
examples: Trusted by 1,200+ GTM teams • 3.8M experiments shipped

terms.title: Testimonials
terms.shortDescription: Longer-form customer quotes paired with names, roles, and outcomes.
terms.definition: Testimonials translate proof into narrative—showing what changed, how fast, and what metric moved.
terms.whenToUse: After value props or near pricing to reinforce belief before commitment.
aiPhrases: Turn this case study into a two-sentence testimonial with a named role and quant result.
examples: “We doubled signups in 45 days once we enforced the attention ratio rules.”

terms.title: FAQ
terms.shortDescription: Answer the top objections before someone bounces to support.
terms.definition: The FAQ clusters 4-6 questions ordered by frequency so teams feel confident clicking the CTA.
terms.whenToUse: Near the bottom or beside pricing when adoption blockers surface.
aiPhrases: List the top five questions a skeptical buyer asks before trying this landing page system.
examples: “How long does setup take?” with a 90-minute reassurance

terms.title: Pricing table
terms.shortDescription: Side-by-side comparison of plans or the single offer summary.
terms.definition: Pricing tables outline cost, inclusions, and commitment so there’s no mystery before the CTA.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever the landing page is selling a specific plan, package, or service tier.
aiPhrases: Compose a single-offer pricing module with price, inclusions, and a risk reducer.
examples: Growth Plan – $2,400/mo • includes CRO lead, playbook, and build crew

terms.title: Footer CTA
terms.shortDescription: Final call-to-action for visitors who read everything.
terms.definition: A mirrored primary CTA paired with contact details or a low-friction alternate action for fence sitters.
terms.whenToUse: Always repeat the CTA at the bottom for high-intent scrollers.
aiPhrases: Write a footer CTA block with a headline, CTA button, and trust microcopy.
examples: Ready to ship cleaner pages? → Book the 20-minute teardown

buckets.title: Design system elements
buckets.description: Tokens, grids, and art direction cues that keep visual polish tied to performance.

terms.title: Hierarchy grid
terms.shortDescription: One grid spec that junior designers can stretch without breaking focus.
terms.definition: A north-star set of columns, gutters, and safe zones that keeps every section flowing hero → proof → CTA.
terms.whenToUse: Before juniors start comping so spacing arguments are settled and feedback centers on story.
aiPhrases: Lay out a hierarchy grid that shows desktop and mobile columns plus safe zones for hero, proof, CTA.
examples: Desktop 10-col grid with 64px margins; mobile 4-col grid guarding a 16px CTA gutter.

terms.title: Type ladder
terms.shortDescription: Three headline rungs and one body style that enforce clarity.
terms.definition: A trimmed type scale with usage notes so every new section instantly signals what to read first.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever a page adds sections or revisions so typography decisions stay plug-and-play.
aiPhrases: Draft a type ladder with Display, Section, Support, and Label styles plus when juniors should use each.
examples: Display 56/64 for hero, Section 32/40 for modules, Support 20/30, Label 13/18 all in the same family.

terms.title: Signal palette
terms.shortDescription: Color tokens named by job (primary, proof, background) not by hex.
terms.definition: A minimal palette that tells juniors which color sells the CTA, which sells proof, and which fades away.
terms.whenToUse: As soon as comps leave grayscale so color never overpowers the CTA or proof badges.
aiPhrases: List signal palette tokens for CTA, proof, depth, and alerts with contrast reminders.
examples: CTA/Emerald 500 on Slate 950, Proof/Amber 400 for badges, Depth/Slate 900 panels.

terms.title: Proof canvas
terms.shortDescription: Reusable framing rules for screenshots, testimonials, and social proof.
terms.definition: Guidelines for shadows, crop, and copy stacking so evidence feels premium and still points back to the CTA.
terms.whenToUse: Before dropping screenshots or quotes into the deck; prevents noisy mockups from hijacking focus.
aiPhrases: Write a proof canvas brief showing how to crop dashboards, stack quotes, and tie them back to the CTA.
examples: Use 12px radius cards, muted gradients, and angled device chrome that leans toward the CTA column.

buckets.title: UX flow playbook
buckets.description: Experience artifacts that keep every interaction confident and conversion-focused.

terms.title: Confidence loop
terms.shortDescription: Sequence that answers what, why, proof, and next in one scroll.
terms.definition: A senior-level checklist to ensure each screen closes the belief gap before asking for the click.
terms.whenToUse: During kickoff or tear-down so juniors know what the page must earn before adding flair.
aiPhrases: Map a confidence loop for this page showing the four beats juniors must hit before the CTA.
examples: Hook → Outcome → Proof → Action with copy and UI cues called out.

terms.title: Decision guardrails
terms.shortDescription: Tiny cues that keep users from wandering off the happy path.
terms.definition: Guidelines for default states, helper text, and progressive disclosure that prevent overwhelm while keeping momentum.
terms.whenToUse: When reviewing wireframes so the team aligns on how much info we reveal at each step.
aiPhrases: Create decision guardrails for the pricing selector so juniors know what shows by default vs on click.
examples: Show one recommended tier by default, tuck comparison rows behind “See plan details.”

terms.title: State telemetry
terms.shortDescription: Feedback pattern that tells users what just happened and what’s next.
terms.definition: Covers validation, loading, and success copy so there is never a dead moment in the flow.
terms.whenToUse: As designs hand off to dev so empty, loading, and success states feel intentional.
aiPhrases: List the telemetry copy and visuals for idle, loading, success, and error around the CTA.
examples: Uploading… progress string, success toast that restates the value, inline fix for errors.

terms.title: Recovery lane
terms.shortDescription: Pre-planned escape hatches that keep users from restarting a flow.
terms.definition: Specifies secondary actions, live chat hooks, or async fallbacks for each critical screen.
terms.whenToUse: When QA spots brittle flows or when juniors script error handling for forms and uploads.
aiPhrases: Design a recovery lane for the brief uploader so users can still submit assets if the file fails.
examples: Offer ‘Email files later’ CTA plus link to guidelines when upload blocks progress.

buckets.title: Vibe coding vocabulary
buckets.description: Plain-English dev words that help non-engineers prompt clearly and ship with AI.

terms.title: Repository (repo)
terms.shortDescription: The home folder for all your project's code and its full history.
terms.definition: A repository stores every file in your project plus a timeline of changes, so you can see what changed, when, and roll back if needed.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever you start a project or tell an AI assistant where the code lives.
aiPhrases: Set up a new Git repository for this project and explain what each generated file does.
examples: A GitHub repo named vibe-guide holding your app code and README.

terms.title: Commit
terms.shortDescription: A saved snapshot of your changes with a short note describing them.
terms.definition: A commit records the current state of your files plus a message, creating a restore point you can return to later.
terms.whenToUse: Each time you finish a small change that works and you want to keep it.
aiPhrases: Write a clear commit message summarizing the change I just made.
examples: "Add contact form validation" as a commit message.

terms.title: Branch
terms.shortDescription: A parallel copy of the project where you can try ideas safely.
terms.definition: A branch lets you experiment without touching the main version; you merge it back only once it works.
terms.whenToUse: Before attempting a risky change or starting a new feature.
aiPhrases: Create a new branch for this experiment so the main version stays safe.
examples: Working on "add-dark-mode" while "main" stays stable.

terms.title: Pull request (PR)
terms.shortDescription: A proposal to merge your branch's changes, open for review first.
terms.definition: A pull request bundles your changes so you or others can review, comment, and approve before they join the main project.
terms.whenToUse: When a branch is ready and you want a checkpoint or review before merging.
aiPhrases: Summarize the changes on this branch into a pull request description.
examples: Opening a PR titled "Add dark mode toggle" for review.

terms.title: Environment variable
terms.shortDescription: A setting or secret stored outside your code, like an API key.
terms.definition: Environment variables hold values that change per environment or must stay private, so secrets never live inside your code.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever you handle passwords, API keys, or settings that differ between local and live.
aiPhrases: Move this API key into an environment variable and show me how to reference it.
examples: Storing OPENAI_API_KEY in a .env file instead of in the code.

terms.title: API
terms.shortDescription: A doorway one app uses to request data or actions from another.
terms.definition: An API (application programming interface) defines how programs talk to each other—what you can ask for and what you get back.
terms.whenToUse: Any time you connect your project to an outside service.
aiPhrases: Explain what this API expects and write the call to fetch the data I need.
examples: Calling a weather API to show today's forecast.

terms.title: Dependency
terms.shortDescription: An outside package your project relies on to work.
terms.definition: A dependency is third-party code you install and build on top of; updating or removing it can change how your app behaves.
terms.whenToUse: When adding a library, or when something breaks right after an update.
aiPhrases: List this project's dependencies and explain what each one does in plain terms.
examples: Next.js and React are dependencies of this app.

terms.title: Deploy (ship)
terms.shortDescription: Push your project live so other people can actually use it.
terms.definition: Deploying takes the version on your machine and makes it available on the internet at a real URL.
terms.whenToUse: When a change is ready to go from "works for me" to publicly live.
aiPhrases: Walk me through deploying this project and what to check before going live.
examples: Deploying to Vercel so the site is reachable at a public URL.

terms.title: Frontend & backend
terms.shortDescription: The part users see versus the part that runs behind the scenes.
terms.definition: The frontend is the visible interface in the browser; the backend handles data, logic, and storage the user never sees directly.
terms.whenToUse: When pointing an AI assistant at the right layer of a problem.
aiPhrases: Is this a frontend or backend problem, and which file should I change?
examples: A button's look is frontend; saving the form to a database is backend.

terms.title: State
terms.shortDescription: The current data an app is holding in memory right now.
terms.definition: State is what the app currently "remembers"—like which tab is open or what a user typed—and changing it updates what's shown.
terms.whenToUse: When something "forgets" what you did or doesn't update on screen.
aiPhrases: Why isn't this updating on screen—walk me through the state involved.
examples: A checkbox staying checked is stored in state.

terms.title: Refactor
terms.shortDescription: Rewrite code to be cleaner without changing what it does.
terms.definition: Refactoring improves the structure or readability of code while keeping its behavior identical.
terms.whenToUse: When code works but is messy, or before building on top of it.
aiPhrases: Refactor this for readability and keep the behavior exactly the same.
examples: Splitting one giant function into smaller, clearly named ones.

terms.title: Edge case
terms.shortDescription: An unusual input or situation that breaks normal assumptions.
terms.definition: An edge case is a rare or extreme scenario—empty input, huge numbers, no internet—that code often forgets to handle.
terms.whenToUse: When reviewing a feature for what could go wrong.
aiPhrases: What edge cases am I missing in this feature, and how should I handle them?
examples: A form that breaks when the name field is left blank.
